intro:
I'm Maya (Esty) Gusak, a math PhD student at Stanford University.

This is a small home for my mathematics, conversations, and occasional writing. Welcome.

math.intro: Notes, questions, and things I'm thinking about in mathematics.

items.title: C1
items.text:
# C1

Have you heard of the phrase "once you finish your PhD, your academic clock starts ticking"? What do you think about it?

Here is the real academic answer to this question that you'll probably hear less often: the academic job is a pretty nice job. You get paid pretty well -- not as well as other jobs you might get with a PhD, but probably better than an average artist, for example; you get to do math all day, meet with students, teach, and paid to travel. It's a pretty cushy job. Unfortunately (or fortunately), there are more people who want this job than there are job openings. So, by the Pigeonhole Principle, there's a lot of competition. If there were less people than job openings, then the academic clock wouldn't matter. But even though there's a lot of stress and competition, you shouldn't forget that 1) you are doing it for a really good job, and 2) it's just a job -- so if it is making you miserable, then you can quit. A lot of people tie their sense of identity to being a mathematician -- this really cool thing of doing math for your whole life -- and I'm certainly not immune to this myself, but the healthy perspective is to remember that this is just a job. So there is no harm in seeing where your life takes you, and making lots of different decisions. It will all be OK.


Best tip for Stanford?

The difference between studying for one qual and studying for two quals is huge. Attempt one qualifying exam upon entry, and take it seriously. Study very hard for two months over the summer, and there's a very good chance you'll pass. There were lots of people who passed both upon entry -- great for them. There were also some people who didn't attempt any qual on the first try, and just passed them on the second try. These people were also successful -- but they were a lot more stressed. You don't lose anything by at least attempting the quals upon entry, and you lose a freebie shot if you don't. Failing an exam is unpleasant, but there's no harm in failing, and there's a chance you'll pass.


Second best tip for Stanford?

The basement offices are the best. They have the windows with the most sunlight and no tourists are walking outside your door, removing potentially awkward encounters.


Third best tip for Stanford?

At any point after you pass your quals, you can apply for a master's degree. It's not as important in the US, but it can matter if you want to come back to Europe. For example, German universities count the total number of degrees you have when considering your application, so you'd need a master's. You might need to write a short thesis, but this shouldn't be a problem in the end.


Let's have one more. Fourth best tip for Stanford?

Your working relationship with your advisor is partially determined by you. Some advisors meet their students more, and some less. If you'd prefer to meet once a week, then you should make this clear with your advisor. You should also meet with your advisor even if you have nothing, and it's just for ten minutes. It's really about giving yourself a deadline.


Have you ever taken a prolonged break from math, and had to recover and "dive back into it"?

Personally, I haven't. But I know a handful of people who have -- including breaks of 1, 3, and 7 years -- and they were able to do it. It's hard, but doable, so don't feel like you're doing something new.

In my personal experience, I went into Stanford as a topologist. When I was visiting, there was a large topology group with great people. But within the time between when I visited and when I started, many of those people left or were unavailable, through a variety of circumstances. That meant I had some time to do some reading courses and try to learn some other math. I took lots of courses, and eventually I took one with a professor who I ended up asking to be my advisor. I really enjoyed reading with him (he's a bit shy), and so I ended up switching to number theory during my second year. This was quite stressful, because I had to catch up on a lot of background that other students in my year seemed to already have. I doubted whether I would get a PhD or not at that point. It was helpful to know that there was this safety net of exiting with a master's degree, though this was never my intention. By the time I was in my fourth and fifth year, I had internalized that, yes, I was getting my PhD. But at that point, I was stressed about applying for jobs -- and I had a two body problem, which was more difficult. So there's always something new to stress about, and the things that you were already stressed about that had worked out already become less important. It's healthy to take a step back and realize that, in this job, there will constantly be things to stressed about. That is one way to motivate yourself, but you shouldn't let it consume you.

items.title: C2
items.text:
# C2

Advice for Stanford?

Quals are difficult -- study hard this summer, but it's like muscle memory, so it'll come back. Don't compare yourself with other people. Other people there will be smarter and better than you, and they'll work harder. It is important to view your PhD as a relationship between you and math.
What was your grad school experience? What went well and what would you change if you had to do it again?
I only met with my advisor six times during my PhD. The first time, it was to ask him to be my advisor. I was very stressed and wanted a flexible advisor. He was so flexible that there was a joke around the department: "if you tell [advisor's name] that you're quitting math to go save kids in Africa, then he'll just smile supportively and say, 'Wonderful!'". 

At the same time, my friend, who was in my year, was also my advisor's student. And every time they had a meeting, my friend would first come into my office and run through all of the proofs that he had worked out during the week. It made me feel that I needed to prove something first before meeting with my advisor. That's why I didn't meet with him for two years! He knew I existed and that I was his student, but we didn't meet until I finally proven something small over the summer. So I go to meet with him, and 20 minutes into presenting my proof, he stops me and goes, "You have your thesis". This taught me to be an independent researcher, but I wish I'd met him more -- I feel I could have learned much more from him, and still been independent.

items.title: C3
items.text:
# C3

How are you?

I'm not doing a lot of math. My students are doing a lot of math. I'm arguing about letting the department keep its whiteboard markers.

What is the difference between industry and academia in post-quantum crypto?

I haven't felt a difference between working in industry and academia. To me it's just working on different parts of the continuous spectrum of cryptography. On one end you have writing papers (for other mathematicians), and on the other, you have writing patents (for lawyers). But it's all part of the same process. Also, I think in 10 years, it won't be "post quantum crypto" anymore. It'll just be "crypto". We'll get there, with quantum computers. Or maybe a secret government agency already got there. And the problem is that, if you're a private business, you can't outsource your cryptography. That's the whole point of being private. So every company will need cryptographers. Nearly all my students go to industry.

Thoughts about living in the US?

The people who voted for Trump who are problematic and you see on the news -- they have already been there for the last 10-20 years already. If you go to West Virginia, it's always been hard to get an abortion there. Trump probably won't get a third term because the Supreme Court, while corrupt, isn't completely corrupt, and they do force him to do things.

How does one choose a field of pure math to study that has "applications"?

Cryptography is a good justification for doing math because, you can basically just translate a hard math problem into a way of encrypting data, and this results in getting a lot of people interested in the math problem. For example, if someone were to say "proving the Riemann Hypothesis is hard. Here's how we're going to translate this into encryption", then a lot of people would study the Riemann Hypothesis. It's very hard to make that translation. Not a lot of people who know really hard math (ex. the 1000s of people who understand the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem) can do simple cryptography, and vice versa. Be good at both! But if you're looking for some justification that isn't cryptography, then it's a good idea to find a way to translate hard math problems into something useful in the real world. Cryptography is just the way I found to do this translation method. Intersectionality and being one of the 5 people in the world who can do a thing makes you a viable candidate for an academic career. There's some things with topological data analysis, neuroscience, protein folding that could be an interesting way to apply geometry.

What was your grad school experiences? What went well and what would you do differently if you had to do it again?

One of my regrets in grad school was thinking that my professors were too much "above me". So I waited until my fourth year to get an advisor. Don't do this. If I had realized this in my second year, I guess I could have graduated in three years, because that's how long it actually took me! :). But at some point I got tired of floundering about in my fourth year, and understood that professors are contractually bound to do what you ask them, (if you are a grad student). That is the point of being in grad school, because they do want you to be there.

Advice for Stanford?

Quals are hard because it's not just about knowing the math, but it's about being able to use the math, and know when a particular theorem is applicable, in order to prove things. Practice a lot.

items.title: C4
items.text:
# C4

Advice for grad school?

Find some people who enjoy math. Surround yourself with people who are smarter than you who you like to work with. Its inspiring. But there will be jerks, so watch out for that. Study for your quals. They don't want you to fail -- but you will certainly need to study. Expect to go to a few seminars each week. People who are very deep into a subject right now tend to do less well. Be willing to learn lots of new things -- that's how research is done. The people who do the best are the ones who are willing to do computations and examples. I do a decent amount of coding (in python). It doesnt have to be good or efficient code; it just needs to run once so that I get the data I need. And we have great fancy computers here! So it really doesn't need to be efficient code. Why do I code to do math? Well, it is much easier to prove results that you know are true.
 
You say that combinatorics is a "school of thought" rather than a field of mathematics. Can you explain?

Eventually, every math proof will boil down to some combinatorics. If it doesn't, then you are just shuffling definitions. As a combinatorist, I am the guy who solves the combinatorics once the other math people boil it down to this part of the problem.
